extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners working on automated reviewer-assignment and peer-review systems (conference chairs, journal editors, grant managers, IR/NLP researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, evaluating, or implementing automated reviewer-assignment (RAP/IRRAP) systems for proposals/submissions, including profile creation, COI detection, and similarity-score computation. Covers manual, text-based (word/semantic), network-based, and neural approaches and their trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profile information sources
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating the proposal's profile, information such as title, keywords, abstract, full text, subject, research/expertise area, references, citation information, co-author information, applicant's institution, discipline/specialty, and applicant-specified keywords can be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three most commonly used information are the proposal's abstract, keyword, and full-text. Full-text usage increased after 2014 (73%) due to advances in high-performance text/word representation techniques in NLP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for Conflict of Interest (COI) detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Detecting potential conflicts of interest between proposals and reviewers is essential to ensure an unbiased and fair proposal evaluation process and must be handled during proposal and reviewer profiling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COIs should be detected and avoided in the assignment task; manual self-declaration is time-consuming and incomplete, motivating automated detection methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definite COIs
rubrics_metrics.description: Definite COIs are explicit relations that can be stated per declaration rules, including co-authorship, colleague relationships, advisee-advisor relationships, project collaborators, and competitor relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly used in conference management systems (e.g., EasyChair) which ask reviewers/authors to disclose such relationships, but self-declaration may be incomplete or overlooked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latent COIs
rubrics_metrics.description: Latent COIs are relationships not required to be declared and must be inferred from explicit relationships (e.g., close friends, academic collaborators, family relatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Latent COIs can be detected using social/academic/professional networks (co-author graphs, institution networks), path-distance measures, weighted relationships, and supervised ranking models (e.g., PISTIS) built from heterogeneous public sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRRAP approach categorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity-score computation approaches (IRRAP) are classified into three categories: (i) manual information-based approach, (ii) text-based/content-based approach, and (iii) network-based approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some studies focus on one category; others combine multiple categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual information-based approaches — Bidding
rubrics_metrics.description: Bidding (rating) asks reviewers to read abstracts or full texts and assign scores representing willingness to review (commonly 3–5 levels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher bidding value indicates higher similarity. Benefits: expert judgment, can improve evaluation quality and reviewer satisfaction. Disadvantages: not scalable with many proposals, sparse bid matrices reduce accuracy, reviewers may bid on current interests rather than cumulative expertise, open to strategic/malicious behavior and COIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual information-based approaches — Expertise keywords/topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers and applicants provide keywords/topics (from a dictionary or free text) representing expertise and proposal content; similarity can be computed by counting common keywords or with Jaccard/Dice similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be combined with reviewer preferences. Self-claimed keywords are subjective and can cause misunderstandings and conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text-based/content-based approaches — Word-based methods (VSM/TF-IDF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vector Space Model (VSM) represents documents as bag-of-words vectors weighted by TF/IDF; similarity (e.g., cosine) between reviewer and proposal vectors is used as the score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: VSM can be effective and straightforward (TF/IDF + cosine). Limitations: lexical matching assumption (words treated independently) loses context and grammar, n-grams mitigate but cause exponential vector-size growth as n increases. Enhancements include keyword extraction and ontology-driven topic mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text-based/content-based approaches — Statistical Language Models (SLM)
rubrics_metrics.description: SLMs use probabilistic/statistical techniques (e.g., language models with Dirichlet smoothing) to model word distributions and predict affinity between reviewer and proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widely used in systems like TPMS. Advantages: probabilistic modeling of terms; disadvantages: data sparsity, curse of dimensionality, and difficulty capturing long-distance dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text-based/content-based approaches — Semantic-based methods: Topic models (LSI/PLSA/LDA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Topic models capture topic distributions in reviewer publications and proposals (examples: LSI/LSA, PLSA, LDA) and compute similarity using topic-space representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LSI is language-independent and computationally straightforward but needs large corpora, lacks probabilistic interpretation, SVD is costly, and choosing topic number is hard. PLSA gives better interpretation but tends to overfit, depends on EM initialization, and scales parameters with documents. LDA provides a generative model and is widely used but assumes a fixed number of topics and topical independence, which can be limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-aware topic models and extensions (ATM, ACT, TET, APT, AST)
rubrics_metrics.description: Author-Topic Model (ATM) and extensions model author information (authors as mixtures of topics) and add layers such as conference/venue, temporal dynamics, persona grouping, and subject hierarchies to better capture author interests and interdisciplinarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATM improves over vanilla LDA by accounting for authorship; extensions (ACT, TET, APT, AST) address venue/time, persona, and subject-sharing to improve matching for temporal trends and interdisciplinary proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other semantic-based / knowledge-enriched methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative semantic approaches include knowledge set theory, Topical Affinity Propagation (II-TAP), fuzzy keyword extraction, fuzzy-graph centrality measures, ontology-based semantic matching, WordNet usage, and semantic kernels built from external resources like Wikipedia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods address shortcomings like short/insufficient abstracts, name ambiguity, and the inability of pure topic models to capture semantic relations. Ontologies and hand-crafted resources improve context but have limited coverage and high maintenance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining word-level and semantic information
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrid approaches integrate word-based (TF/IDF, SLM) and semantic/topic-based (LDA) representations to compute similarity scores, sometimes adding time-awareness and exact + semantic matching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining methods (e.g., LDA + SLM, TF/IDF + LDA) often yields more accurate similarity scores by leveraging complementary strengths; examples include time-aware topic models and integrated exact/semantic matching scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neural network-based language models
rubrics_metrics.description: Neural language models (Word2Vec, Doc2Vec, BERT, SciBERT, CNN, biLSTM, etc.) produce dense contextualized representations encoding semantic and syntactic affinities used for similarity computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although less common as of 2018, neural models have shown superior performance to other semantic methods in some studies and are promising for future similarity-score computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal weighting / recency of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers' more recent publications better reflect current research interests; models can be time-aware to prioritize recent work when modeling expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time-aware topic modeling or weighting recent publications (e.g., temporal-expert-topic) can improve matching accuracy for reviewers whose interests evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling author name ambiguity and reviewer identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Name ambiguity complicates extracting accurate reviewer profiles from publication records, potentially harming candidate selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools like Peer2ref use co-authorship information to disambiguate authors; cross-checking multiple data sources (ArnetMiner, DBLP, ScholarMate, ORCID) is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling reviewer expertise levels with fuzzy sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Expertise can be modeled as linguistic variables or fuzzy sets (triangular fuzzy numbers, type-2 fuzzy sets) rather than crisp values to capture uncertainty and field-dependent variation in competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fuzzy extraction and automatic keyword extraction combined with fuzzy-graph centrality and extension principles can yield richer similarity measures when expertise is hard to express crisply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sparsity, scalability, and high-dimensionality issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical problems include sparse bidding matrices, high-dimensional sparse vectors (curse of dimensionality), computationally expensive SVD updates for LSI, and scalability when the number of proposals grows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These issues reduce assignment accuracy and increase computation; methods need to address sparsity (e.g., hybrid methods, automatic profile enrichment), dimensionality (embedding-based or topic-model dimensionality reduction), and computational cost (efficient updates or approximate methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted-relationship and heterogeneous-data approaches for COI and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Using weighted heterogeneous associations (co-authorship, co-working duration, affiliations, advisor-advisee) to construct a publication/academic network and using supervised ranking or factor-graph models to infer relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PISTIS and similar systems retrieve heterogeneous public sources (DBLP, affiliation histories) and recommend latent COIs via supervised ranking models iteratively updated with historical declarations; weighted relations help detect latent COIs where ground truth is scarce.
